title: Wood frogs can survive with ice inside their bodies
body: A wood frog can spend winter partly frozen, with **no heartbeat or breathing**, then become active again after thawing. Ice forms outside its cells, while its liver releases large amounts of glucose, a sugar that helps protect the cells from freezing and losing water. This lets the frog overwinter in leaf litter on the forest floor. The crucial trick is controlling where ice forms, rather than freezing every cell solid.

left.label: Outside cells
left.text: Ice can form between tissues and around organs during the frog's winter freeze.

right.label: Inside cells
right.text: Protective substances help keep cell interiors from freezing and limit dehydration.

slides.heading: A winter survival sequence
items: Cooling triggers ice formation and the release of protective glucose.
Heartbeat and breathing stop as the frog freezes.
Warming allows thawing, followed by the return of body functions.

slides.heading: Frozen does not mean dead
slides.text: This is a specialized survival adaptation. The frog remains alive through conditions that would kill most animals.

source.label: National Park Service: Wood Frog — Biological Miracle
